summary: Defines an aggregation and fragmentation mode for IPsec ESP. It lets many small IP packets share one ESP packet, or one large packet span several. The main goal is IP Traffic Flow Security: hiding the size and timing of the real traffic from observers who can see the encrypted tunnel.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of mailing many small envelopes of different sizes, you ship same-sized boxes at a steady pace, so spies cannot guess what you are sending.

questions: how to hide traffic patterns in ipsec
subtitle: A fixed-size, constant-rate ESP tunnel that packs and splits IP packets so observers cannot read traffic patterns.

tldr.problem: Encryption hides the content of IP packets, but their sizes and timing can still reveal information. Padding each ESP packet to hide this wastes a lot of bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: AGGFRAG mode sends fixed-size ESP packets at a constant rate. Each one can carry whole, partial or several inner IP packets, with padding only when no data is waiting. An optional congestion-controlled mode adjusts the rate.
tldr.outcome: IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS) provides full Traffic Flow Confidentiality without the bandwidth limits of RFC 4303 padding, and is expected to reduce the efficacy of traffic analysis on IPsec communication.

facts.label: Header size
facts.value: 4 octets, or 24 octets with congestion control

today: RFC 9347 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. YANG and MIB documents for IP-TFS are defined in RFC 9348 and RFC 9349.

sections.title: Hiding the Shape of Traffic
sections.content:
Traffic analysis extracts information from the shape and timing of message traffic even when the data itself is encrypted. Hiding the size and frequency of traffic is called Traffic Flow Confidentiality (TFC), the term used in RFC 4303.

RFC 4303 offers TFC by allowing padding on encrypted IP packets and by allowing all-pad packets (protocol 59). The major limitation is that this can significantly underutilize the available bandwidth, because only one IP packet can be sent per encapsulating packet.

This RFC defines an aggregation and fragmentation (AGGFRAG) mode for ESP and its use for IP-TFS. It uses a constant-send-rate IPsec tunnel with fixed-size encapsulating packets, which can contain partial, whole or multiple IP packets. A nonconstant send rate is allowed, but its confidentiality properties are outside the scope. The mechanisms are generic, but non-TFS uses are also out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Even in sealed envelopes, a spy can learn things from how many envelopes you send and how big they are. Sending same-sized boxes at a steady pace gives the spy nothing to read.

sections.title: The AGGFRAG Tunnel
sections.content:
The AGGFRAG tunnel uses an IPsec tunnel as its transport. The main input is the requested bandwidth. From it come two values: the fixed size of the encapsulating packets and the rate at which to send them. The packet send rate is the requested bandwidth divided by the encapsulating packet size.

The fixed size MAY be configured manually or found with Packetization Layer MTU Discovery (PLMTUD) or Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD). PMTUD is known to have issues, so PLMTUD is considered more robust. The receiving side MUST allow for the sender varying the size and rate unless policy constrains it.

Padding is added only if no data is available at transmission time, or if the receiver has disabled fragmentation. Like normal ESP, AGGFRAG SAs are unidirectional, so bidirectional IP-TFS needs two SAs, one in each direction. A sender MUST only send AGGFRAG_PAYLOAD payloads over an SA configured for AGGFRAG mode.
sections.plainLanguage: You pick how much stuff to ship per second. The tunnel then picks a box size and sends one box at a steady beat, adding filler only when there is nothing to put in.

sections.title: Data Blocks, Fragmentation and Reassembly
sections.content:
An AGGFRAG payload starts with a header, 4 octets or 24 octets, followed by DataBlocks. A data block starts with a 4-bit type chosen to match the IPv4/IPv6 version field, so no per-block type overhead is needed. Its length comes from the inner IPv4 Total Length or IPv6 Payload Length. The BlockOffset field points to the start of the next new data block. If it is zero, the DataBlocks start with a new block. If it points past the end, the next block starts in a later packet. This lets a receiver recover the next inner packet after outer packet loss.

To allow reassembly, a sender MUST send fragments of an inner packet back to back using consecutive ESP sequence numbers. It MAY insert all-pad payloads between them. Sequence numbers MUST increase monotonically by 1, and a sender MUST NOT send initial fragments on one SA and later fragments on another. Receivers need a reordering window, with a value of 3 suggested as a default, and the size SHOULD be configurable. A lost packet timer is RECOMMENDED.

A receiver MAY pass inner packets on as soon as they are complete, which can amplify out-of-order delivery, or MAY reorder first, which adds delay when a packet is lost. The sender MAY pad out an outer packet to avoid fragmenting an inner one, at a cost in tunnel capacity.

Pad Data Blocks are never fragmented, so after a payload that ends with one, the next BlockOffset MUST be zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Big items are cut up and put in consecutive boxes, small ones share a box. Each box has a note saying where the next new item begins, so one lost box does not ruin everything.

sections.title: Modes of Operation and Congestion Control
sections.content:
IP-TFS has two modes. In the non-congestion-controlled mode the packet rate is constant and never adjusts to congestion. It MUST only be used where the user has full administrative control over every path the tunnel takes, and MUST NOT be used otherwise. Packet loss should be reported to the administrator, and circuit breakers are RECOMMENDED.

In the congestion-controlled mode the sender lowers the rate when there is congestion and raises it when congestion subsides. No specific algorithm is required, but best current practice RECOMMENDS one that conforms to RFC 5348. Its inputs are the receiver's loss event rate and the sender's estimated round-trip time (RTT).

The receiver sends this information back on its own SA, so it MUST have a paired SA to the sender. The sender puts a timestamp in TVal, and the receiver echoes it in TEcho with an Echo Delay and a Transmit Delay. The sender computes two RTT estimates and SHOULD use the larger. Congestion information MUST be sent at least once per RTT. A "no feedback timeout" equals 4 RTT intervals and halves the sending rate. IP-TFS is not reliable delivery, so there are no per-packet acknowledgements.

With ECN enabled, a packet arriving with Congestion Experienced set counts as dropped. The sender SHOULD use the "compatibility" mode of RFC 6040 and set the outer ECN field to Not-ECT.
sections.plainLanguage: One mode is a train on its own private track at a fixed speed. The other is a car in traffic that slows down when the road is jammed and speeds up when it clears.

sections.title: Payload Formats
sections.content:
AGGFRAG_PAYLOAD is identified by ESP Next Header value 144. The first octet is a sub-type. Sub-type 0 is the non-congestion-control format with a 4-octet header: Sub-Type, a Reserved octet, and a 16-bit BlockOffset. Sub-type 1 is the congestion control format with a 24-octet header.

The congestion control header adds P (PLMTUD probing in progress) and E (CE ECN bits were used) flags, a 32-bit LossEventRate carrying the inverse of the loss event rate (zero means no loss), a 22-bit RTT in microseconds, 21-bit Echo Delay and Transmit Delay values, and 32-bit TVal and TEcho values.

Data block type 0x0 is a Pad Data Block, 0x4 an IPv4 data block and 0x6 an IPv6 data block. Padding extends to the end of the encapsulating packet. An empty payload (header only) can carry congestion information on an SA that is not AGGFRAG enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: Each box has a small label up front. It says what kind of box it is, where the next new item starts, and sometimes how crowded the road is.

sections.title: Negotiating with IKEv2
sections.content:
With IKEv2, a new USE_AGGFRAG notification enables AGGFRAG_PAYLOAD on a Child SA pair, similar to how USE_TRANSPORT_MODE is negotiated in RFC 7296. The initiator includes it when requesting a new Child SA. If the responder accepts, its response MUST include the same notification. If it declines, the Child SA is created without AGGFRAG, and the initiator MUST delete it if that is unacceptable. USE_AGGFRAG MUST NOT be combined with USE_TRANSPORT, since only non-transport-mode tunnels are defined.

The notification carries one octet of flags. The C bit requires that congestion control information be returned periodically. The D bit says the sender cannot receive packet fragments. The notify status type is 16442.

IP-TFS configuration is meant to be minimal and lives on the unidirectional ingress side. Non-IKEv2 operation is intended to work with local static configuration. Bandwidth, packet size and congestion control are local options with no standardized configuration method required.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the box method, the two sides ask each other if they both know it. If one says no, they use the ordinary way instead.

sections.title: Security and Overhead
sections.content:
The mechanism is expected to reduce the efficacy of traffic analysis on IPsec communication. Beyond that, the security considerations of RFC 4303 and RFC 7296 apply.

ECN bits are not protected by IPsec and may constitute a covert channel, so ECN use SHOULD NOT be enabled by default. For TFC to hold, the encapsulated traffic should not affect network congestion in a predictable way. If it would, non-congestion-controlled mode should be considered.

Appendix C compares overhead using AES-GCM-256, where IP plus ESP overhead is 54 octets. With the 4-octet non-congestion-control AGGFRAG header, the total is 58 octets per outer packet. The IP-TFS overhead as a percentage of inner packet size is 5800 divided by the outer payload size. The RFC tabulates it as 11.20%, 4.02% and 0.65% for MTUs of 576, 1500 and 9000.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing is perfect. Some small signals can still leak if you are careless, and the extra labels cost a little space, but they cost much less than sending nearly empty boxes.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 on generation and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: BlockOffset
fields.desc: Octets of DataBlocks data before the start of a new data block.

items.label: Pad Data Block
items.desc: Padding that extends to the end of the encapsulating packet.

items.label: IPv4 data block
items.desc: Starts with an inner IPv4 packet; length from Total Length.

items.label: IPv6 data block
items.desc: Starts with an inner IPv6 packet; length from Payload Length.

messages.label: Accept with USE_AGGFRAG
messages.note: If declined, the Child SA is made without AGGFRAG.
